title: Nepal PM Urges Calm as Curfew Holds After Sectarian Clashes Kill Three
excerpt: Several towns in southeastern Nepal remain under indefinite curfew after Hindu-Muslim violence erupted over a dispute involving loud music and religious flags during a Hindu event.
body:
• Three people have been killed and 25 injured in sectarian clashes between Hindus and Muslims in southeastern Nepal since Sunday
  • Violence was triggered by a dispute over loud music and religious flags during a Hindu event in Diwanganj, Sunsari district
  • Several towns remain under indefinite curfew as Nepal's Gen Z-backed PM Balendra Shah appeals for calm
  • Home Minister Sudan Gurung visited families of victims and agreed to provide roughly $6,660 in relief to each

Several towns in southeastern Nepal remained under indefinite curfew on Friday as authorities worked to contain tensions after days of sectarian violence between Hindu and Muslim communities that have left at least three people dead.

The unrest erupted on Sunday in Diwanganj, a town in Nepal's Sunsari district near the Indian border, after a dispute over loud music and religious flags during a Hindu event escalated into violent clashes. Twenty-five people were injured in the late-night confrontation, police said.

Three Dead Across Two Districts

Two men were shot and killed in Sunsari on Sunday. A third death was reported in neighbouring Siraha district on Thursday as sporadic clashes continued to flare across the region. Police spokesperson Abi Narayan Kafle said all incidents were under investigation.

No further violence was reported on Friday, but the curfew remained in place across several towns as a preventive measure.

PM Shah's Rare Address

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah, the 35-year-old rapper-turned-politician who swept to power on a wave of Gen Z support after last year's revolution, delivered a rare televised address to the nation on Thursday, urging people to remove the "cloud of turbulence" from the Himalayan nation.

"The government will conduct a fair and impartial investigation into the violence and punish those responsible for the trouble in a transparent way."

— Balendra Shah, Prime Minister of Nepal

Home Minister Sudan Gurung traveled to Sunsari to meet the families of the two killed there, and the government agreed to provide approximately $6,660 in relief to each family. Gurung was expected to visit Siraha on Friday to meet the family of the third victim.

A Fragile Moment for Nepal

The violence comes at a sensitive time for Nepal, which is still recovering from the upheaval of September 2025, when Gen Z-led anti-corruption protests forced the resignation of former PM K.P. Sharma Oli after security forces killed at least 76 protesters. The protests brought down the government and led to new elections that swept Shah and his Rastriya Swatantra Party into power.

Sectarian violence is relatively rare in Nepal, where Hindus make up roughly 81 percent of the population and Muslims about 5 percent. The two communities have historically coexisted with little friction, making the current clashes particularly alarming for a country trying to rebuild institutional trust.

For the Indian diaspora and the significant cross-border communities along the Nepal-India border, the unrest raises concerns about regional stability and the safety of nationals in the area. Nepal's Sunsari district shares a porous border with India's Bihar state, and movement between the two countries is routine.
